docs.title: IFU to Instruction TLB Interface
docs.text:
FILE:    itlb_ifu_interfaces.md
 SOURCE:  session-069
 STATUS:  DRAFT
 UPDATED: 2026-10-09
 CONTACT: Jeff Nye

Owns the IT-N registry.

docs.title: 1. Scope
docs.text:
Two groups cross this boundary: the IFU asks the ITLB to translate a virtual address, and the ITLB answers.

The requester is the IFU's TRANSLATION pipeline, ifu_decisions.md IFU-24, which runs ahead of the fetch pipeline and queues its results. It is not F0 of the fetch pipeline. Nothing in this document depends on which of the two it is, but a reader placing these ports in the fetch stages would put them in the wrong pipeline. The ITLB's own miss path into the page table walker is not here; it is itlb_l2tlb_interfaces.md. This read "into the shared L2 TLB"; there is no L2 TLB now (mmu_decisions.md MMU-1), session-077.

docs.title: 2. The groups
docs.text:
ifu_itlb_req_val                        IFU  -> ITLB
  ifu_itlb_req_rdy                        ITLB -> IFU
  ifu_itlb_vpn   [VA_WIDTH-13:0]          IFU  -> ITLB
  ifu_itlb_tag                            IFU  -> ITLB

  itlb_ifu_rsp_val                        ITLB -> IFU
  itlb_ifu_tag                            ITLB -> IFU
  itlb_ifu_status [1:0]                   ITLB -> IFU
  itlb_ifu_ppn   [PPN_WIDTH-1:0]          ITLB -> IFU
  itlb_ifu_cause [CAUSE_WIDTH-1:0]        ITLB -> IFU
  itlb_ifu_gpa   [FAULT_GPA_WIDTH-1:0]    ITLB -> IFU
  itlb_ifu_gpa_imp [1:0]                  ITLB -> IFU
  itlb_ifu_pma   [PMA_WIDTH-1:0]          ITLB -> IFU

IT-16 `ifu_itlb_vpn` is VA_WIDTH - 12 = 29 bits, the fetch
      address above the page offset, not VPN_WIDTH (27). With V=1
      and vsatp.MODE=Bare the fetch PC is a 41-bit guest physical
      address, and with V=0 and satp.MODE=Bare a fetch address
      above bit 35 must reach the PMA check to fault (FE-19). A
      27-bit port drops both. Ruled session-074 (Jeff); this read
      [VPN_WIDTH-1:0]. The IFU port is built at this width on
      both lookups by BP-117, TD#146 closed.

IT-1  One request port. A block that crosses a page needs two
      translations and they are issued on successive cycles, not
      on a second port.

IT-2  `ifu_itlb_tag` is one bit and names which half of the block
      the request covers. 0 is the block's own page, 1 is the
      page the straddle reaches into.

IT-3  The response carries the tag back. Responses may return out
      of order, so the tag is how the IFU attributes them.

IT-1 is the reason IT-3 exists. Two requests are in flight when a block crosses a page, the first can miss while the second hits, and the hit returns first. A second request port would avoid the tag at the cost of a second set of 64 comparators against the fully associative array of ITLB-2, spent on a case that occurs only at a page boundary.

docs.title: 3. The result
docs.text:
IT-4 itlb_ifu_status is three-way, which is ITLB-11.

  2'b00   hit    ppn valid, cause and the block's PMA valid
  2'b01   miss   a walk has started. ppn and cause are invalid.
  2'b10   fault  cause valid. ppn invalid.
  2'b11   reserved

  A reserved status, or a fault whose cause is not 1, 12 or
  20, is treated by the IFU as an instruction access fault.
  Session-074, as BP-116 built it.

IT-5  The virtual address the fault applies to is not returned.
      The IFU supplied it and holds it. Returning it would give
      one fact two producers.

IT-6  `itlb_ifu_cause` distinguishes three causes: instruction
      access fault, cause 1, from the PMP or PMA check of MMU-10
      and MMU-12; instruction page fault, cause 12, from a
      single-stage or VS-stage translation; and instruction
      guest-page fault, cause 20, from the G-stage. H is
      mandatory in RVA23 through Sha, so the third is not
      optional.

IT-6a `itlb_ifu_gpa` carries the faulting GUEST PHYSICAL address
      and is valid only when the cause is 20. Shtvala requires
      `htval` to be written with it, and unlike the virtual
      address of IT-5 the IFU never had it: it is produced inside
      the walk. So it returns here and IT-5 does not apply to it.
      It is FAULT_GPA_WIDTH = 56 bits (mmu_decisions.md MMU-23).
      For kind 00 the ITLB passes the walker's page and the IFU
      fills the offset (ifu_decisions.md IFU-2a). This was
      [GPA_WIDTH-1:0]. Ruled session-077 (Jeff), after BP-123;
      BUILT by BP-124.

IT-6b Nothing about the translation regime is on this port. The
      IFU presents a virtual address and no more.

  The ITLB reads what it needs directly: the V bit, the ASID
  and the VMID for the tag match of ITLB-4 and ITLB-4a, and
  the MODE fields to know whether translation is enabled or
  Bare.

  IT DOES NOT READ THE ROOT POINTERS. The ITLB does not walk,
  so `satp.PPN`, `vsatp.PPN` and `hgatp.PPN` are no use to it.
  They belong to the walker, `itlb_l2tlb_interfaces.md` IL-3c
  and mmu_decisions.md MMU-24a. An earlier revision of this
  rule had the ITLB read all three; until session-077 this
  placed the walker inside an L2 TLB.

IT-6c `itlb_ifu_gpa_imp` is the implicit-access kind of
      `itlb_l2tlb_interfaces.md` IL-11b, valid with IT-6a: 2'b00
      the fetch's own guest physical address, 2'b01 an implicit
      read of a VS-stage page table, 2'b10 an implicit write of
      one, 2'b11 reserved. The ITLB passes it through from the
      walker, holding it with a held fault (ITLB-10a). The IFU
      carries it into `ifu_pd_pkt_t` beside the GPA (DCD-16); the
      backend needs it for htinst (mmu_decisions.md MMU-29). Added
      session-077 (Jeff).

IT-5 is a departure from how ITLB-11 is worded. That rule has the ITLB return the fault cause and the faulting virtual address together, because the pair is what must reach the backend under Sstvala. The pair is assembled in the IFU: it already holds the VA, it receives the cause here, and it carries both into ifu_pd_pkt_t at IB-9 (DCD-16; this read predecode_pkt_t until session-074). Nothing is lost and the VA does not make a round trip.

docs.title: 4. Miss
docs.text:
IT-7  A miss response ends the transaction. The ITLB does not
      hold the request and does not answer it later.

IT-8  The IFU re-requests. It may re-request in any cycle after
      the miss response and the ITLB does not require a minimum
      interval.

IT-9  A re-request for a virtual address with a walk already in
      flight receives a miss response and starts no second walk.
      The ITLB matches against its in-flight walks. This is
      ITLB-10 and it is stated here because the IFU's behaviour
      depends on it: the IFU may re-request freely and cannot
      cause duplicate walk traffic.

docs.title: 5. PMA
docs.text:
IT-10 `itlb_ifu_pma` returns the attributes of MMU-13 on a hit,
      at the bit positions MMU-13 fixes: [0] cacheable,
      [1] coherent, [2] executable, [3] idempotent. They are the
      EFFECTIVE attributes: the region table combined with the
      entry's PBMT, the most restrictive of the two
      (mmu_decisions.md MMU-U6, ITLB-3a). Executable and coherent
      come from the region table alone.

IT-11 The IFU reads cacheable and idempotent to decide the path. A
      fetch with both set is an ordinary L1I request; otherwise it
      is an UNCACHED L1I request (ifu_decisions.md IFU-21,
      l1i_ifu_interfaces.md IF-44), presented only under the commit
      gate of IFU-22, and never allocates in the L1I (MMU-14). So a
      page marked NC or IO never allocates in the L1I. This read
      "otherwise it takes the uncached path of IFU-21 and does not
      reach the L1I"; IFU-21 reversed session-076. Before that it
      read "The IFU reads idempotent" against the region alone.
      Session-071.

IT-12 A PMP or PMA failure arrives ON THIS RESPONSE as status
      fault, cause 1. The checker instance beside the ITLB
      (mmu_decisions.md MMU-10a, MMU-10b) evaluates the translated
      address, and the IFU consumes the result before it issues an
      L1I request; it does not check. On a hit `itlb_ifu_pma` is
      the effective attributes of IT-10, which decide the cached
      or uncached path (IT-11). ITLB-12 and ITLB-12a.

  This read that the checks do not gate this response and that
  the IFU consumes "the PMP and PMA results" from it, which
  left where a denial appears unstated; BP-118 built it as
  cause 1, as MMU-10b already said. Ruled session-075 (Jeff).

IT-12a No L1I request is issued for a block that fails PMP or
       PMA. `l1i_ifu_interfaces.md` IF-22: a faulting request
       never reaches the L1I and that interface has no fault port
       in either direction. The translation pipeline of IFU-23a
       is what makes this free; there is no cycle to save by
       letting the request go and killing the response.

docs.title: 6. Flow control
docs.text:
IT-13 `ifu_itlb_req_rdy` deasserts when the ITLB cannot accept a
      lookup. The IFU holds the request stable until it is taken.

IT-14 The response has no ready. The IFU accepts every response
      in the cycle it is presented. It has a slot for each of the
      two outstanding requests IT-1 permits and cannot run out.

docs.title: 7. Maintenance
docs.text:
IT-15 SFENCE.VMA does not cross this boundary. ITLB-14 gives the
      ITLB a distinct invalidate port and the IFU is not on that
      path.

docs.title: 8. Open
docs.text: None here. Two items elsewhere bear on this port without changing it: the in-flight walk tracker depth, ITLB-U1, closed by ITLB-15 at a parameter of 1 with the walker performing one walk at a time (MMU-U2), and IT-9 holds at any depth. This read "bounded by TD#118"; session-077. IFU-U5, the translation queue depth that sets how far ahead of the fetch pipeline these requests are issued, was closed session-074 at a parameter of 4; a page-crossing block issues its two lookups on successive cycles (IFU-25, IT-1).

docs.title: 9. Bindings
docs.text: ITLB-2 The fully associative array IT-1 avoids duplicating. ITLB-5 One cycle hit, preserved by IT-12. ITLB-8 Non-blocking, IT-7. ITLB-9 The requester re-requests, IT-8. ITLB-10 In-flight walk match, IT-9. ITLB-11 Three-way result, IT-4. The VA half is IT-5. ITLB-12 Check placement, IT-12. ITLB-14 Invalidate port, IT-15. IFU-7 Two lookups per block, IT-1 and IT-2. IFU-21 The uncached path IT-11 selects. MMU-13 The attributes of IT-10. IB-9 Where the cause and VA are paired. MMU-29 The implicit-access kind of IT-6c.

docs.title: 10. Document History
docs.text:
2026-10-09  session-077, rulings (Jeff). IT-6c and
              itlb_ifu_gpa_imp, the implicit-access kind. Section 1
              and IT-6b: the walker is the ITLB's server, with no
              L2 TLB (MMU-1 reversed). This document had no history
              section; its earlier changes are in PROJECT_STATUS.

  2026-10-09  session-077, after BP-123, ruling (Jeff). IT-6a:
              itlb_ifu_gpa is FAULT_GPA_WIDTH = 56.

  2026-10-10  session-077, after BP-124. IT-6a built.

docs.title: Instruction TLB to L2 TLB Interface
docs.text:
FILE:    itlb_l2tlb_interfaces.md
 SOURCE:  session-069
 STATUS:  DRAFT
 UPDATED: 2026-10-15
 CONTACT: Jeff Nye

Owns the IL-N registry.

docs.title: 1. Scope
docs.text:
Two groups cross this boundary: the ITLB presents a miss, and the server answers with a translation or a fault.

THE SERVER IS THE PAGE TABLE WALKER. There is no L2 TLB now (mmu_decisions.md MMU-1, reversed session-077); an ITLB miss goes to the walker directly. The port was written for an L2 TLB and its shape is unchanged: a walker also holds the transaction open until the walk completes (IL-5). An L2 TLB added later sits behind this same port. THE PORT NAMES KEEP l2t, ruled session-077 (Jeff): they are built, and renaming them buys nothing a reader of this paragraph needs. Where the rules below say L2 TLB, read the walker until an L2 TLB exists.

The walk itself, the walker's memory port, and the A and D bit handling are mmu_decisions.md and ptw_mem_interfaces.md.

The L1 data TLB will be a second client of this same port shape. Nothing here is I-side specific and the port is written to be instantiated twice.

docs.title: 2. The groups
docs.text:
itlb_l2t_req_val                        ITLB   -> walker
  itlb_l2t_req_rdy                        walker -> ITLB
  itlb_l2t_vpn   [VA_WIDTH-13:0]          ITLB   -> walker
  itlb_l2t_asid  [ASID_WIDTH-1:0]         ITLB   -> walker
  itlb_l2t_vmid  [VMID_WIDTH-1:0]         ITLB   -> walker
  itlb_l2t_v                              ITLB   -> walker
  itlb_l2t_tag   [1:0]                    ITLB   -> walker
  itlb_l2t_acc   [1:0]                    ITLB   -> walker
  itlb_l2t_priv  [1:0]                    ITLB   -> walker

  l2t_itlb_rsp_val                        walker -> ITLB
  l2t_itlb_tag   [1:0]                    walker -> ITLB
  l2t_itlb_status [1:0]                   walker -> ITLB
  l2t_itlb_ppn   [PPN_WIDTH-1:0]          walker -> ITLB
  l2t_itlb_size  [2:0]                    walker -> ITLB
  l2t_itlb_perm  [PERM_WIDTH-1:0]         walker -> ITLB
  l2t_itlb_pbmt  [1:0]                    walker -> ITLB
  l2t_itlb_cause [CAUSE_WIDTH-1:0]        walker -> ITLB
  l2t_itlb_gpa   [FAULT_GPA_WIDTH-1:0]    walker -> ITLB
  l2t_itlb_gpa_imp [1:0]                  walker -> ITLB

The far end is the page table walker (section 1). This list read L2TLB at the far end (DOC-002, D9). Session-080.

IL-1a `itlb_l2t_vpn` is VA_WIDTH - 12 = 29 bits, for the reason
      itlb_ifu_interfaces.md IT-16 gives for the IFU side: with V=1
      and vsatp.MODE=Bare the address is a 41-bit guest physical
      address, and a 27-bit field drops bits 40:39. BP-118 built
      it at 29. This read [VPN_WIDTH-1:0]. Session-075.

IL-1  `itlb_l2t_tag` is two bits. Up to four requests may be
      outstanding from one client. The walker accepts one at a
      time (MMU-U2, closed session-077) and answers others retry,
      IL-6; the tag width is unchanged.

IL-2  The response carries the tag back. Responses may return out
      of order.

Two bits covers the two translations IT-1 allows in flight on the I side and leaves headroom. The tracker depth is a separate decision, ITLB-U1, and can change without touching this port. Sizing the tag to the tracker would couple them.

IL-3  The translation context IDENTITY travels with the request:
      the V bit, the ASID and the VMID. The L2 TLB does not hold a
      current ASID or VMID; the client already holds both for its
      own tag match, so sending them keeps one producer.

IL-3c THE MMU DOES READ CSRs. IL-3 is about identity, not about
      the whole CSR file. What the WALK needs is regime state and
      is read directly, not carried per request:

  satp.PPN                 single-stage root
  vsatp.PPN, hgatp.PPN     VS-stage and G-stage roots, MMU-19
  the MODE fields          whether translation is on, and Bare
  menvcfg.ADUE             Svade against Svadu, MMU-7
  henvcfg.ADUE             the same for the VS-stage, MMU-7a
  menvcfg/henvcfg.PBMTE    the PBMT walker checks, MMU-U6

These reach the walker on its own CSR input group, not through the front-end top (mmu_decisions.md MMU-24a). The root pointers are narrower than the architectural fields (MMU-24b).

The division is that identity is a property of the REQUEST and the regime is not. A root pointer is not something one request has and another does not, and putting it on the port would make every client a producer of it.

AN EARLIER REVISION OF IL-3 said the L2 TLB does not read a CSR, full stop. That contradicted MMU-7 and MMU-7a, which already have the MMU read the ADUE bits, and it left the walker with no source for the root it walks from. Session-069.

IL-3a The VMID and the V bit travel with it for the same reason.
      H is mandatory in RVA23 through Sha, so a request is either
      a `V=0` single-stage translation or a `V=1` two-stage one,
      and a two-stage request names its guest. ITLB-4a.

IL-3d THE ACCESS TYPE AND THE PRIVILEGE travel with the request,
      as identity does, because they are properties of one
      request (mmu_decisions.md MMU-24c). `itlb_l2t_acc` is 0
      read, 1 write, 2 execute, 3 reserved; the ITLB always
      presents execute. BP-123 built it on the walker only (D2),
      tied to execute in tb_fe_top, accepted session-077; BP-124
      has the ITLB drive it and fe_top carry it.
      `itlb_l2t_priv` is 2'b00 U or 2'b01 S, with `itlb_l2t_v`
      the effective privilege the walker checks a leaf's U bit
      against before setting A (MMU-8c). Ruled session-077 (Jeff);
      BUILT by BP-124. 2'b10 (reserved) and 2'b11 (M) are never
      presented. SUM and MXR join the request with the DTLB.

IL-3b A `V=1` request commits the walker to a NESTED walk,
      MMU-21, which is several times the work of a single-stage
      one. The port does not distinguish them beyond the V bit;
      the cost difference is the walker's to absorb and is why
      IL-6 exists. This read "the L2 TLB"; session-077.

docs.title: 3. The result
docs.text:
IL-4 l2t_itlb_status is three-way.

  2'b00   hit    ppn, size and perm valid
  2'b01   fault  cause valid, ppn invalid
  2'b10   retry  no walk was started, re-request
  2'b11   reserved

IL-5  There is no miss status. An accepted request starts a walk
      and the response is deferred until the walk completes. The
      transaction stays open. This is the opposite of ITLB-8,
      where a miss ends the transaction and the requester
      re-requests. This read "An L2 TLB miss starts a walk";
      session-077.

IL-6  `retry` is not a miss. It means the walker could not accept
      the request, because it is performing another walk
      (MMU-U2), so nothing is in flight and the client must ask
      again. It exists because IL-5 makes the transaction
      long-lived. This read "into its tracker" of an L2 TLB;
      session-077.

IL-5 is why this port differs from the one above it. The ITLB answers the IFU immediately because the IFU has other work and a prediction block to abandon. The ITLB has nothing else to do with a missed translation, so holding the transaction open costs it nothing and saves a re-request path.

This read "a fetch block to abandon"; the fetch block is the 64-byte L1I line (fe_decisions.md Conventions). Session-071.

docs.title: 4. Page size and permissions
docs.text:
IL-7  `l2t_itlb_size` names which page size the translation
      covers: 4 KiB, 64 KiB (Svnapot), 2 MiB or 1 GiB. THREE bits,
      RULED session-075 (Jeff): 3'b000 4 KiB, 3'b001 64 KiB,
      3'b010 2 MiB, 3'b011 1 GiB, 3'b1xx reserved for a future
      size. Ascending, so a larger code always masks more VPN
      bits. BP-118 built two bits; BP-119 widened to three. A
      response that hits with a reserved size code is handled as a
      reserved status (IT-4, IL-4), built by BP-119. The ITLB
      installs the entry at that size, ITLB-3; a 64 KiB entry is
      held once with a masked match (mmu_decisions.md MMU-U7).
      The PPN returned for a 64 KiB page is the PTE's, with
      PPN[3:0] the size marker; the ITLB substitutes on its
      output. This read "which of the three Sv39 page sizes".
      Session-071.

IL-7a For a `V=1` translation the size is the SMALLER of the two
      stages' leaf sizes, and the PPN is the final supervisor
      physical page at that size (mmu_decisions.md MMU-27).
      Session-077. Built by BP-123: the PPN is the final page for
      the request's address (D7, accepted session-077).

IL-8  `l2t_itlb_perm` carries the PTE permission and attribute
      bits the ITLB must hold to answer later hits without asking
      again. Included are the executable, user and global bits.
      The global bit sets the ITLB entry's global flag of
      ITLB-4. For a G-stage-only translation (V=1, vsatp.MODE
      Bare) it is the G-stage leaf's byte with G cleared, and the
      ITLB does not apply ITLB-16 to it (mmu_decisions.md MMU-31).
      Built by BP-123 (D7), accepted session-077.

IL-9  The PMA attributes of MMU-13 are not returned here. They
      come from the static region table and are a function of the
      physical address, so the ITLB derives them from the PPN it
      was given rather than being told.

IL-9 is a placement choice and it follows MMU-15 for the attributes the region table decides. Svpbmt is mandatory in RVA23S64, so the PTE's PBMT field is a second memory type source, per translation, that the region table cannot supply (mmu_decisions.md MMU-U5). This paragraph said a PMA "is a property of an address range, not of a translation" and that returning one would make the L2 TLB "a second source for something the region table already decides", which MMU-U5 contradicts. Session-071.

IL-9a `l2t_itlb_pbmt` returns the page's memory type on a hit: the
      more restrictive of the G-stage and VS-stage PBMT, ordered
      PMA < NC < IO, and PMA (2'b00) when neither stage sets one.
      The ITLB stores it (ITLB-3a) and combines it with the region
      attributes into the effective type, the most restrictive of
      the three (mmu_decisions.md MMU-U6, ruled session-071). A
      reserved PBMT, or a non-zero one with PBMTE clear, never
      reaches this port: the walker faults it.

docs.title: 5. Faults
docs.text:
IL-10 A fault response ends the transaction. The cause
      distinguishes three: a page fault from a single-stage or
      VS-stage walk, a GUEST page fault from the G-stage, and an
      access fault. MMU-16. The access fault has five sources: the
      PMP check the walker makes on every access (MMU-10, MMU-10d),
      the PMA check on every access (MMU-12), a page table outside
      cacheable coherent memory (MMU-12a), a PPN naming an address
      this implementation cannot form (MMU-28), and an error from
      the walker's memory port (ptw_mem_interfaces.md WM-7). This
      named the PMP check only; session-077.

IL-11 The faulting virtual address is not returned. The client
      supplied it and holds it against the tag.

IL-11a The faulting GUEST PHYSICAL address IS returned on
       `l2t_itlb_gpa`, valid on a guest page fault only. The
       client never had it; it is
       produced inside the nested walk. Shtvala requires `htval`
       to carry it. This is the one address that travels back on
       this port, and it continues to the IFU as
       `itlb_ifu_gpa`, IT-6a. It is FAULT_GPA_WIDTH = 56 bits and
       carries every faulting GPA whole (mmu_decisions.md MMU-23).
       For kind 00 (IL-11b) the walker returns the page and the
       IFU fills the offset. Ruled session-077 (Jeff), after
       BP-123; BUILT by BP-124. This read "It is 0 when the
       faulting guest physical address does not fit GPA_WIDTH
       (MMU-30)"; MMU-30 is withdrawn.

IL-11b `l2t_itlb_gpa_imp` says what the GPA is, valid on a guest
       page fault only: 2'b00 the fetch's own guest physical
       address, 2'b01 an implicit read of a VS-stage page table,
       2'b10 an implicit write of one (the Svadu update), 2'b11
       reserved. The backend needs it to write htinst, which must
       be a pseudoinstruction for an implicit-access fault with a
       non-zero htval (mmu_decisions.md MMU-29). It continues to
       the IFU as `itlb_ifu_gpa_imp`, IT-6c. Added session-077
       (Jeff).

docs.title: 6. Maintenance
docs.text:
IL-12 SFENCE.VMA does not cross this boundary, and neither do
      HFENCE.VVMA and HFENCE.GVMA, nor the Svinval instructions,
      which act as those three (mmu_decisions.md MMU-U8). The ITLB
      has its own invalidate port, ITLB-14. The walker has none,
      because it holds no translation (MMU-17); an L2 TLB, when
      added, has its own (MMU-18). Neither forwards to the other.
      MMU-17a.

IL-13 A walk in flight when an invalidate arrives completes. The
      walker installs nothing in any case; an L2 TLB, when added,
      does not install the result. MMU-17. Whether the response is
      still returned to the client, or suppressed so the client's
      tracker entry must time out, is the one thing this port must
      state and IL-14 states it.

IL-14 The response is returned normally. The client installs
      nothing, because a client that received an invalidate in
      the same window discards its own tracker entry. A
      suppressed response would leave the client's tag allocated
      with nothing to release it.

docs.title: 7. Open
docs.text: None. MMU-U6, MMU-U7 and MMU-U8, which reached IL-7, IL-9 and IL-12, were ruled session-071; IL-9a adds l2t_itlb_pbmt. MMU-U9 was ruled session-077; IL-10, IL-11a and IL-11b carry it.

docs.title: 8. Bindings
docs.text:
ITLB-3    Page sizes, IL-7.
ITLB-4    ASID and global, IL-3 and IL-8.
ITLB-8    Contrasted by IL-5.
ITLB-10   The in-flight match that keeps duplicate requests off
          this port.
ITLB-14   The ITLB invalidate port, IL-12.
ITLB-U1   Tracker depth, decoupled from IL-1 by design.
IT-1      Two outstanding I-side translations, the sizing input
          to IL-1.
MMU-3     The L1 TLBs are clients of this port.
MMU-10    The walker's PMP check, the access-fault cause of IL-10.
          This read "the second cause"; IL-10 lists it third.
          Session-071.
MMU-13    PMA attributes, deliberately absent by IL-9.
MMU-15    The static region table IL-9 defers to.
MMU-17    Invalidate during a walk, IL-13 and IL-14.
MMU-18    The L2 TLB invalidate port, when there is one, IL-12.
MMU-1     No L2 TLB now; the walker is the server, section 1.
MMU-27    The two-stage size, IL-7a.
MMU-29    The implicit-access kind, IL-11b.
MMU-23    FAULT_GPA_WIDTH, IL-11a.
MMU-24c   The access type and privilege, IL-3d.
MMU-31    The G-stage-only permission byte, IL-8.

docs.title: 9. Document History
docs.text:
2026-10-09  session-077, rulings (Jeff). The server is the walker,
              not an L2 TLB (MMU-1 reversed); the port names keep
              l2t. l2t_itlb_gpa_imp and IL-11b added. IL-7a, the
              two-stage size. IL-10 names every access-fault
              source. IL-1, IL-3b, IL-5, IL-6, IL-12 and IL-13
              restated for a walker. This document had no history
              section; its earlier changes are in PROJECT_STATUS.

  2026-10-09  session-077, after BP-123, rulings (Jeff). IL-3d:
              itlb_l2t_acc as BP-123 built it (on the walker only;
              BP-124 has the ITLB drive it), and itlb_l2t_priv.
              IL-11a: l2t_itlb_gpa is FAULT_GPA_WIDTH = 56, the
              zero sentinel withdrawn. IL-8: the G-stage-only
              permission byte.

  2026-10-10  session-077, after BP-124. IL-3d and IL-11a built.

  2026-10-15  session-080, after DOC-002. Section 2: the far end is
              the walker.

docs.title: Page Table Walker to Memory Interface
docs.text:
FILE:    ptw_mem_interfaces.md
 SOURCE:  session-077 rulings; mmu_decisions.md MMU-2, MMU-8
 STATUS:  DRAFT
 UPDATED: 2026-10-09
 CONTACT: Jeff Nye

Owns the WM-N registry.

docs.title: 1. Scope
docs.text:
The page table walker's port to memory (mmu_decisions.md MMU-2). The walker reads PTEs on it and performs the Svadu update of MMU-8 on it. Nothing else uses it.

TODAY A TESTBENCH ANSWERS IT. There is no L2 (Jeff, session-076), so tb_fe_top's memory model answers this port, from the same memory image as the model that answers the L1I's memory port (fe_decisions.md FE-21). The port is still real RTL on the walker, specified as the permanent boundary: when an L2 exists the walker's traffic goes on a master edge into it (MMU-2), and how the compare-and-swap of WM-5 is carried there is mmu_decisions.md MMU-U3.

The client side of the walker is itlb_l2tlb_interfaces.md. The walk itself is mmu_decisions.md.

docs.title: 2. Naming
docs.text:
ptw_mem_<signal>    walker -> memory
  mem_ptw_<signal>    memory -> walker

No stage suffixes, as for l1i_ifu_interfaces.md 2.

docs.title: 3. Ports
docs.text:
ptw_mem_req_val                              walker -> memory
  ptw_mem_req_rdy                              memory -> walker
  ptw_mem_req_op                               walker -> memory
  ptw_mem_req_paddr  [PA_WIDTH-1:0]            walker -> memory
  ptw_mem_req_cmp    [63:0]                    walker -> memory
  ptw_mem_req_swap   [63:0]                    walker -> memory

  mem_ptw_rsp_val                              memory -> walker
  mem_ptw_rsp_data   [63:0]                    memory -> walker
  mem_ptw_rsp_err                              memory -> walker

  ptw_mem_req_op   0  READ   read the 8 bytes at paddr
                   1  CAS    compare and swap the 8 bytes at paddr

There is no response ready, no identifier and no byte enable.

docs.title: 4. Rules
docs.text:
WM-1  EVERY ACCESS IS ONE PTE: 8 bytes, naturally aligned, and
        atomic. ptw_mem_req_paddr[2:0] is zero. The privileged
        specification performs every implicit access to the
        translation structures at PTESIZE, which is 8 for Sv39 and
        Sv39x4, and an A/D update rewrites the whole PTE, not one
        bit of it. The memory side asserts the alignment.

  WM-2  A request is accepted in a cycle where ptw_mem_req_val and
        ptw_mem_req_rdy are both high. The walker holds every
        request field stable from the cycle val rises until
        acceptance. ptw_mem_req_rdy does not depend combinationally
        on ptw_mem_req_val.

  WM-3  AT MOST ONE REQUEST IS OUTSTANDING, from acceptance until
        its response. The walker performs one walk at a time
        (mmu_decisions.md MMU-U2) and each step of a walk needs the
        previous PTE, so a second request would have nothing to
        carry.

  WM-4  The response is presented when mem_ptw_rsp_val is high, no
        earlier than the cycle after acceptance. The walker accepts
        it unconditionally in that cycle. WM-3 makes an identifier
        unnecessary.

  WM-5  CAS COMPARES AND STORES AS ONE ATOMIC OPERATION. The memory
        compares the 8 bytes at paddr with ptw_mem_req_cmp; if they
        are equal it stores ptw_mem_req_swap there. In either case
        mem_ptw_rsp_data returns the value the memory held BEFORE
        the operation, so the walker knows the store happened
        exactly when mem_ptw_rsp_data equals ptw_mem_req_cmp. No
        other access to those bytes may fall between the compare
        and the store. This is the privileged translation
        algorithm's step 9 (mmu_decisions.md MMU-8): on a mismatch
        the walker restarts the walk.

  WM-6  A CAS RESPONSE IS NOT PRESENTED BEFORE THE STORE IS VISIBLE
        to every later access by any agent. The walker returns the
        translation only after this response (MMU-8), so the update
        precedes the fetch that needed it in the global order, as
        the specification requires.

  WM-7  mem_ptw_rsp_err high with mem_ptw_rsp_val means the memory
        side returned an error. mem_ptw_rsp_data is then undefined,
        and for a CAS nothing was stored. The walker reports an
        access fault, cause 1, for the translation it was
        performing. The memory side's error has the same standing
        as l1i_ifu_interfaces.md IF-15.

  WM-8  A REQUEST THAT FAILS A CHECK IS NEVER PRESENTED. The walker
        makes the PMP and PMA checks of mmu_decisions.md MMU-10d,
        MMU-12 and MMU-12a, and refuses an address it cannot form
        (MMU-28), before it presents the request, so no checked
        failure reaches this port. The same division as
        l1i_ifu_interfaces.md IF-22.

  WM-9  While rstn is low the walker holds ptw_mem_req_val low and
        the memory side holds mem_ptw_rsp_val and ptw_mem_req_rdy
        low. Nothing is outstanding across reset.

docs.title: 5. The testbench memory model
docs.text:
What tb_fe_top's model must do on this port, because the programs BP-123 writes depend on it:

  WM-10 ONE MEMORY IMAGE. The model answering this port and the
        model answering the L1I's memory port read and write one
        store, so a page table written by the program's set-up and
        a later instruction fetch see the same bytes, and an A bit
        set by the walker is visible to a later walk.

  WM-11 IT CAN CHANGE A PTE BETWEEN A WALK'S READ AND ITS CAS, on
        the stimulus's instruction, so the mismatch path of WM-5
        and the restart of MMU-8 are exercised. An agent writing
        memory between the two is exactly the case the compare
        exists for.

  WM-12 IT CAN RETURN mem_ptw_rsp_err on a chosen access, read or
        CAS, so WM-7 is exercised.

  WM-13 IT CAN HOLD ptw_mem_req_rdy LOW and vary the response
        latency, so the walker is not tested against one fixed
        timing.

docs.title: 6. Open
docs.text: None. The L2 half of the compare-and-swap is mmu_decisions.md MMU-U3, moved to the L2 work.

docs.title: 7. Bindings
docs.text:
MMU-2     The port this document specifies.
  MMU-8     The CAS of WM-5 and the ordering of WM-6.
  MMU-10d   The checks of WM-8, at privilege S.
  MMU-12a   Page tables only in cacheable coherent memory, WM-8.
  MMU-28    Addresses the walker cannot form, WM-8.
  MMU-U2    One walk at a time, the basis of WM-3.
  MMU-U3    The L2 realisation of WM-5.
  FE-21     The L1I memory port whose model shares WM-10's image.
  IL-*      The walker's client side, itlb_l2tlb_interfaces.md.

docs.title: 8. Document History
docs.text:
2026-10-09  Created, session-077, from the rulings that reversed
              MMU-1 and confirmed full Svadu (Jeff). The walker has
              its own memory port, answered by a testbench model
              until an L2 exists. One request outstanding, 8-byte
              READ and CAS, a CAS response only once the store is
              visible, checks made before the request.

docs.title: Showcase
docs.text: A showcase release is documentation built around testcases and waveforms. Each page follows one program through the RTL and explains what the waveform shows. It is not a specification; the design is described in the architecture pages and the planning documents.

docs.title: Release 01: Frontend Demo
docs.text:
Release fe-1.0.0. The Showcase pages are taken from the release tag fe-1.0.0. The hosted waveforms are published from the same tag; their manifest.json names it.

Twenty-four short programs run on the Pacino frontend, fe_top, with testbench models of the backend, the page table walker and memory. Each scenario shows one behavior: prediction and override, the predictors, redirects, the L1I, translation and faults, compressed code, uncached fetch, cache maintenance, backpressure and commit. Each run ends in a PASS or FAIL line and writes an FST waveform. The Frontend Overview describes the design. How a Scenario Is Built and Run covers the testbench, the program writer and how to read the waveforms.

Select either diagram to open it at full size. The signal annotations on the block view refer to the fe_top connectivity inventory.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
From examples/fe_demo/:

make <scenario>          run one scenario; writes out/<scenario>/
make scenarios           run all 24 in order
make view S=<scenario>   open the scenario's waveform in Surfer
make help                list the scenarios

It needs Verilator 5.048 and, for make view, Surfer; the repository README covers installing both.

docs.title: CSR Decisions
docs.text:
FILE:    csr_decisions.md
 SOURCE:  session-079, TD#178
 STATUS:  DRAFT
 UPDATED: 2026-10-14
 CONTACT: Jeff Nye

Owns the CSR-N and CSR-UN registries.

docs.title: 1. Organization
docs.text:
CSR-1  rtl/core/csr/rtl/csr_pkg.sv declares, for each CSR in
       sections 2 and 3:
         CSR_<NAME>_ADDR   12-bit localparam
         <name>_t          packed struct, full XLEN layout
         encodings         MODE values, PMP A-field values
         reset value
       and the three group structs of section 4.

CSR-2  rtl/core/csr/tb/csr_tb_pkg.sv (testbench only) holds a
       shadow of every CSR in csr_pkg and provides:
         csr_write(addr, value)   applies the write rules of CSR-5
         csr_read(addr)
         pack functions           shadow -> fe_cfg_t, fe_csr_t,
                                  ptw_csr_t
         csr_reset()              every CSR, priv, V and
                                  ext_enable to reset (CSR-7)
         set_ext_enable(v)        ext_enable has no address
         set_priv(p), set_v(v)    priv and V have no address
         set_pmp_g(g)             grain of the read-back rules; 10
                                  unless a PMP checker testbench
                                  builds another PMP_GRAN_LG2
         named setters            each field of 0x7C0 and 0x7C1
       The shadow is a class with static members behind these
       package functions. An address with no CSR in csr_pkg stops the
       simulation ($fatal).
       Every testbench that drives a group member takes its value
       from csr_tb_pkg. Testbenches of fe_top, the ITLB, the PMP
       checker and the walker drive the struct ports from the pack
       functions; testbenches of other modules drive their existing
       ports from the struct members.

docs.title: 2. Custom CSRs
docs.text:
Machine-level read/write, range 0x7C0-0x7FF.

  0x7C0   CSR_7C0, predictor enables
  bit     field                when 1
  0       sc_enable            SC participates in prediction and update
  1       ftb_fastpath_en      saturated FTB counter may commit at p2
  2       tage_enable_aging    TAGE useful-counter aging runs
  3       ittage_enable_aging  ITTAGE useful-counter aging runs
  63:4    reserved, read 0, writes ignored

  0x7C1   CSR_7C1, aging intervals
  bits    field
  31:0    tage_aging_interval
  63:32   ittage_aging_interval

CSR-3  sc_enable = 0: no SC update is issued, the SC prediction
       response is not consumed or waited on, SC-related FTB state
       is still buffered. PROPOSED.

CSR-4  ext_enable is not a CSR and has no address. It is a member of
       fe_cfg_t of type decode_pkg::ext_enable_t (one enable per
       decoded extension), set only through set_ext_enable, reset
       RVA23_ENABLE (all ones). Clearing a bit makes decode treat that
       extension as illegal; such a configuration is not RVA23.

docs.title: 3. Standard CSRs
docs.text:
XLEN 64. Fields as defined in [PRIV]; the table gives the implemented subset. Bits not listed read 0.

  addr   CSR       field   bits    implemented
  0x180  satp      MODE    63:60   0 Bare, 8 Sv39
                   ASID    59:44   16 bits
                   PPN     43:0    23:0 (PPN_WIDTH 24)
  0x280  vsatp     MODE    63:60   0 Bare, 8 Sv39
                   ASID    59:44   16 bits
                   PPN     43:0    28:0 (GPA_WIDTH 41 - 12)
  0x680  hgatp     MODE    63:60   0 Bare, 8 Sv39x4
                   VMID    57:44   14 bits
                   PPN     43:0    23:0; 1:0 read 0 in Sv39x4
  0x30A  menvcfg   PBMTE   62
                   ADUE    61
  0x60A  henvcfg   PBMTE   62      read 0 when menvcfg.PBMTE = 0
                   ADUE    61      read 0 when menvcfg.ADUE = 0
  0x3A0  pmpcfg0   entries 0-7, one byte each:
  0x3A2  pmpcfg2   entries 8-15  L 7, A 4:3, X 2, W 1, R 0
                                   A: 0 OFF, 1 TOR, 3 NAPOT
                                   (NA4 not selectable, G = 10)
  0x3B0- pmpaddr0  ADDR    53:0    33:0 (PA_WIDTH 36)
  0x3BF  -15

priv and V are hart state, not CSRs. priv encoding: 00 U, 01 S, 11 M.

CSR-5 csr_write rules:

  satp     unsupported MODE: no field written
  hgatp    unsupported MODE: MODE unchanged, VMID and PPN written
  vsatp    unsupported MODE: no field written. PROPOSED
  pmpcfg   locked entry (L = 1): entry and its pmpaddr not written
           A = NA4 written: stored as NAPOT
           R = 0 with W = 1 written: stored with W = 0
  pmpaddr  not written when the next entry is locked with A = TOR
           read-back with G = 10: NAPOT entry, bits 8:0 read 1;
           OFF or TOR entry, bits 9:0 read 0
  henvcfg  PBMTE read 0 when menvcfg.PBMTE = 0
           ADUE read 0 when menvcfg.ADUE = 0
  all      unimplemented bits read 0

   Read-0 rules apply at csr_read and in the pack functions; the
   stored bit is kept.

docs.title: 4. Group structs and RTL connection
docs.text:
CSR-6  fe_top and the ITLB take fe_csr_t, fe_top takes fe_cfg_t and
       the walker takes ptw_csr_t, as whole-group ports. The PMP
       checker takes pmpcfg and pmpaddr, entries 0 to PMP_ENTRIES-1,
       as csr_pkg pmpcfg_ent_t and pmpaddr_imp_t arrays; its
       privilege input is not a group member (the walker's site
       checks at S). Inside fe_top the members drive the existing
       ports of the consumers below. Member names are the former
       port names without the csr_itlb_ or csr_ptw_ prefix.

  fe_cfg_t   source: 0x7C0, 0x7C1, ext_enable
  member                  consumer
  sc_enable               bp_cluster, FTQ (sc carries the port,
                          unused)
  ftb_fastpath_en         bp_cluster (FTB fast path)
  tage_enable_aging       tage
  tage_aging_interval     tage
  ittage_enable_aging     ittage
  ittage_aging_interval   ittage
  ext_enable              decode

  fe_csr_t   source: satp, vsatp, hgatp, pmpcfg, pmpaddr, priv, V
  member                  consumer
  v, priv                 ITLB, ITLB PMP checker (priv only)
  satp MODE, ASID         ITLB
  vsatp MODE, ASID        ITLB
  hgatp MODE, VMID        ITLB
  pmpcfg[16], pmpaddr[16] ITLB PMP checker

  ptw_csr_t  source: satp, vsatp, hgatp, menvcfg, henvcfg, pmpcfg,
             pmpaddr
  member                  consumer
  satp, vsatp, hgatp
    MODE, PPN             walker
  menvcfg ADUE, PBMTE     walker
  henvcfg ADUE, PBMTE     walker
  pmpcfg[16], pmpaddr[16] walker PMP checker

   fe_top takes fe_cfg_t and fe_csr_t and distributes the
   members above. The walker is outside fe_top and takes
   ptw_csr_t directly. The walker samples the MODE, PPN, ADUE
   and PBMTE members at the start of each walk; its PMP checker
   reads pmpcfg and pmpaddr every cycle.

CSR-7 Reset values (csr_reset):

  0x7C0     0x1                  sc_enable 1, the other three 0
  0x7C1     0
  satp      0x0000_0000_0008_F000  MODE Bare, ASID 0, PPN 0x8F000
  vsatp     0
  hgatp     0
  menvcfg   0x4000_0000_0000_0000  PBMTE 1, ADUE 0
  henvcfg   0x4000_0000_0000_0000  PBMTE 1, ADUE 0
  pmpcfg0   0x1F                 entry 0 NAPOT RWX, entries 1-7 OFF
  pmpcfg2   0
  pmpaddr0  0x3_FFFF_FFFF        every implemented bit
  pmpaddr1-15  0
  priv      11 (M)
  V         0
  ext_enable  RVA23_ENABLE (all ones)

docs.text:
CSR-U1 Names of the CSRs at 0x7C0 and 0x7C1.
CSR-U2 Hardware delivery of CSR state to the groups, and ordering
       of a CSR write against fetch, SFENCE.VMA, HFENCE, FENCE.I.

docs.title: Scenario Common Description
docs.text:
This document explains the operation of the functions used by the scenarios:

  • the program writer
  • the instruction list
  • the backend model
  • results console status

A glossary of frontend terms is included at the end.

examples/fe_demo/ holds the collateral files used by the scenarios.

Full path Shorthand Explanation examples/fe_demo/docs docs/ demo descriptions examples/fe_demo/programs programs/ scenario drivers examples/fe_demo/tb tb/ demo specific testbench support examples/fe_demo/waves waves/ Surfer signal files

The shared testbench models are found in rtl/core/frontend/fe_top/tb/models/, shortened to models/ below.

docs.title: 1. The scenario
docs.text:
A scenario exercises isolated aspects of the Pacino frontend (FE). The full scenario list is found in planning/showcase/fe_demo_scenarios.md, numbered FD-1 to FD-24. Each scenario has an associated make target in examples/fe_demo/Makefile. The targets are of the form fdNN_<name>.

A scenario has three files, the "program", the wave control file and the writeup:

  • programs/fdNN_<name>.svh
    • contains the task prog_fdNN which populates the model's memory and begins execution.
    • In the demos there is no assembly step; the instructions are written to model memory directly as instruction words.
  • waves/fdNN_<name>.sucl
    • this is a Surfer command file containing signals, groups and markers
    • Events in the waveforms are annotated using these markers. The markers are also described in the scenario description.
  • docs/fdNN_<name>.md
    • the scenario description.

A run has four steps:

  1. begin_scen prints the start line and resets all models and the monitors.
  2. The program task writes the program and the expected instruction list to the model memory.
  3. demo_go releases reset and runs until every expected instruction has retired. The pipeline runs for a number of cycles to allow the pipeline to flush.
  4. The top level evaluates the scenario's correctness and prints the results.

The scenario top level testbench is tb/tb_fe_demo.sv. This testbench instantiates the FE as fe_top, and the page table walker.

The plusarg +SCEN=<name> selects the scenario and run_scen in tb/tb_fe_demo.sv calls its prog_fdNN task.

There are two simulation models, based on the number of prediction slots selected. NUM_PRED_SLOTS selects 1 or 2 prediction slots. Pacino's FE runs either.

NUM_PRED_SLOTS=1 is used for the simpler explanations to reduce the amount of data and the number of signals that must be recorded.

Full performance, NUM_PRED_SLOTS=2, scenarios are included to show dual prediction operation. NUM_PRED_SLOTS=2 is the configuration used for performance analysis.

FD-3, FD-22, FD-23 and FD-24 run the dual prediction model.

Fast initialization. The predictor tables need an initial value before they can predict. In the design, TAGE, ITTAGE and SC each walk their tables after reset, writing one entry per cycle, and raise a ready when the walk ends: ITTAGE at cyc 513, SC at cyc 1025 and TAGE at cyc 2049 (FD-1). The FTQ holds its p0 request (u_ftq.u_npc.w_hold) until all three readies are high.

Every scenario except FD-1 skips the table initialization walk. The Makefile passes +TAGE_FAST_INIT=1 +ITTAGE_FAST_INIT=1 +SC_FAST_INIT=1 (FE_FAST_INIT, rtl/core/frontend/fe_top/fe_top_srcs.mk). With these, a SystemVerilog initial block in each table writes its initial values at time 0, and each predictor ties its ready to 1 (tage.sv line 333, and the same mux in ittage.sv and sc.sv). Prediction starts on the first cycle after reset instead of about 2048 cycles later.

One effect shows in the waveforms: with the readies 1 from time 0, ftq_pred_val_p0 is already 1 while tb.rstn is low. Nothing captures the request until reset is released, and the first p1 prediction is at cyc 1.

docs.title: 2. The program writer
docs.text:
The program writer builds the memory image and the expected execution list.

The memory image is a byte array indexed by physical address. The expected execution list is the sequence of instructions the program retires, in order. The backend model checks each retired instruction against the list (section 3).

The memory model services instruction cache line requests from the memory image. The page table walker reads from this image.

Scenarios run either in machine mode with physical addresses or in supervisor mode under Sv39 translation. For the Sv39 scenarios, the writer also builds the page tables in the memory image. FD-14 and FD-15 also use two-stage (guest) translation.

The program writer includes tasks which emit either 16b or 32b instructions. The writer emits either "filler" or "active" instructions.

The filler instructions serve to position an active instruction at a particular PC. The PCs are varied to set up configurations which illustrate operation of the frontend.

The active instructions are branches or jumps, plus fence.i, cbo.inval and a store used in FD-13 and FD-19. Filler instructions are variations of addi. The emitters write filler instructions, branches, etc.; demo_go terminates each program with an instruction which jumps to itself, a halt.

The memory image is written before reset is released.

The writer appends each instruction to the expected execution list only if it executes. Instructions skipped by a taken branch are in the memory image but not in the execution list, and a loop appears in the list once per iteration.

Each branch's direction is set by the program when it writes the branch. Register values are never computed (section 3), so a branch's comparison has no effect on its direction: the testbench controls the taken/not taken decision of a branch.

In FD-09 and FD-11 some branch directions are randomized in order to illustrate predictor behavior under those conditions; the testbench uses an LFSR to randomize the taken/not taken state.

docs.title: 3. The expected execution list
docs.text:
The testbench does not model the instruction set. The expected execution list is the reference instead. This list contains the instructions the program retires, in order. The backend model retires an instruction when it matches the next entry (section 4).

Each entry holds the instruction's address and encoding, its control-transfer type, its direction and its target. A fetch fault or a trap the program expects is also an entry. The entry type is ex_t in models/fe_tb_writer.svh.

docs.title: 4. The backend model
docs.text:
The backend is an abstract model. It does not execute instructions. The backend model accepts up to 8 instructions from the frontend via decoder port tb.pd_out and checks these instructions against the expected execution list and retires them in order. The backend model raises tb.dec_ibuf_rdy when it is ready to accept more instructions.

A prediction determines which instruction the frontend fetches after a branch or jump. The model checks the prediction by comparing the next instruction delivered with the next entry in the expected execution list.

If they match, the prediction was correct, and the model reports the branch's outcome, its direction and target, to the FTQ on tb.bkend_ftq_rsv.

If they do not match, the frontend has fetched down the wrong path. The backend model reports the outcome marked as a misprediction, discards the rest of the delivered group, and raises a redirect, tb.bkend_ftq_redir_val, to the expected address. The frontend flushes its younger work and fetches from that address. This is the backend misprediction the scenario descriptions refer to; its cycle is the cycle bkend_ftq_redir_val is high.

The backend model also commits FTQ entries whose instructions have all retired (tb.bkend_ftq_commit_val, tb.bkend_ftq_commit_idx).

Any other mismatch, for example an instruction with the wrong encoding, is a stream error: the model prints a line that begins ERROR: and the run fails (section 5).

The plusarg +TRACE makes the backend print a line for each retired instruction and each misprediction, with the cycle count first. These lines are for debugging and do not follow the result-line format.

docs.title: 5. The result line
docs.text:
To maintain stability in the scenarios, they are developed against tagged versions of the RTL. The Showcase landing page specifies the current tag. The scenarios run internal checks to verify that the waveforms and scenario descriptions match the current state of the design.

A run passes when every expected instruction retires with no stream error and the scenario's checks pass. It writes a result line to its log, out/<scenario>/<scenario>.log, prints one console line, -I: <scenario> : PASS : cyc = <n>, and exits with status 0. Otherwise it writes a failing result line, prints -E: <scenario> : FAIL : cyc = <n> and exits non-zero, which stops make scenarios.

A result line begins with -I: (information), -W: (warning) or -E: (error), then the scenario name. A passing line gives PASS, the counts the checks read, and cyc, the number of cycles from the release of reset to the last retirement:

-I: fd09_tage: PASS, tagged-provider predictions 188, allocations 59,
    T0 by use_alt_on_na 22, cyc 1364

When the expected instructions did not all retire, the failing line says so first:

-E: fd09_tage: FAIL, stream not retired, retired 1200 of 1510,
    stream errors 1, ...

The ERROR: lines for stream errors and the +TRACE debug lines (section 4) use a different format.

docs.title: 6. The cycle counter cyc
docs.text:
tb.cyc counts clock cycles from the release of reset and is shown next to the clock in every waveform.

Scenario descriptions give times as values of cyc. An event "at cyc N" occurs in the clock period in which tb.cyc shows N; a register written in that period shows its new value from cyc N + 1.

docs.title: 7. Reading the waveforms
docs.text:
Each scenario description has an "Open waveform" link that opens the scenario in Surfer in the browser.

From the command line, make view S=<scenario> opens it in a local Surfer session (README.md, section 2).

Surfer shortens signal names to the end of their hierarchical path. The scenario descriptions give the full path in Surfer's form, which names an array element by its index under the array, for example tb.dut.u_bpu.u_tage.u_tage_cntrl.uaon.[0].

A one-slot waveform shows slot 0 of each per-slot signal; a two-slot waveform shows slots 0 and 1. Encoded fields, such as trx_type, are shown as numbers; the descriptions that show one give its encoding.

A scenario whose description has an event table opens with one marker per event, named c<cyc>_<label>, in a group named markers immediately after the clock group, and the view at the first marker. The Events table is section 5 of the description, and section 6 lists the waveform's signals.

docs.title: 8. Glossary
docs.text:
Standard RISC-V terms (Sv39, Sv39x4, VS-stage and G-stage translation, PBMT, PMP, Svadu, link registers) are used as the specifications define them. The entries below give Pacino's parameters, conventions and signal names.

Term Description allocation (TAGE) On a TAGE misprediction of a conditional branch, a new entry is written in the first table with a longer history than the primary's whose entry at the branch's index has an aged useful value of 0. The candidate is chosen at prediction time; if no table qualifies, nothing is allocated. The new entry gets the branch's tag and a CTR of 3'b100. alternate (TAGE) The matching tagged table with the next shorter history below the primary, or T0 when no such table matches. Table number tage_alt_comp in the prediction metadata, 0 for T0. back edge The branch at the end of a loop body that jumps back to the loop's first instruction. It is taken on every iteration but the last, on which it falls through. backend model The testbench's stand-in for the backend (section 4). It retires in program order against the expected execution list, sends resolutions, redirects and commits, and does not execute instructions. block The prediction and fetch unit: at most 32 bytes from a start address, ending at the first predicted-taken control transfer. A 32-bit instruction starting in the last halfword is delivered with the block, which then spans 34 bytes. An FTB entry holds at most one branch per prediction slot; a block with more branches is split at update, ending the entry at the first branch it cannot hold (FD-23). One FTQ entry per block. BPU tb.dut.u_bpu: uBTB, loop predictor, FTB, TAGE, ITTAGE, SC and RAS, and the per-stage logic that combines their predictions. branch type bp_br_type_e, as shown in the waveforms: COND, DIRECT_UNC (jal, rd not a link register), DIRECT_CALL, INDIRECT_CALL (push only), RETURN, RETURN_CALL (jalr with rd and rs1 both link registers and unequal: pop then push), INDIRECT_NONRET and NO_BRANCH. Call and return classification follows the RISC-V link-register hints. bundle Decode's output per cycle, up to eight instructions on tb.pd_out, accepted when tb.dec_ibuf_rdy is high. cbo.inval, fence.i cbo.inval invalidates the cache line holding a given address; fence.i makes earlier stores visible to instruction fetch. At retirement of either, the backend model drives the frontend's commit-stage maintenance port and restarts fetch after the acknowledgment (FD-13, FD-19). commit The backend model raises tb.bkend_ftq_commit_val as its retirement watermark advances; the FTQ commit pointer follows one entry per cycle, freeing entries and committing RAS state for their calls and returns. CTR 3-bit saturating direction counter in tagged TAGE entries, its top bit the prediction: 3'b100 to 3'b111 taken, 3'b000 to 3'b011 not taken. 3'b011 and 3'b100 are weak, 3'b000 and 3'b111 strong. Updates step by one toward the resolved direction. fall through A branch falls through when it is not taken: execution continues at the next instruction. frontend tb.dut: BPU, FTQ, IFU, L1I, instruction buffer and decode. FTB Fetch target buffer: per block start, the block's end and its branches with positions, types and targets. Answers at p2. FTQ Fetch target queue, tb.dut.u_ftq, one entry per predicted block. Issues prediction requests, holds predictions and their metadata, feeds the IFU, and takes resolutions, redirects and commits from the backend. G-stage, VS-stage, two-stage translation Address translation for a guest running under a hypervisor. The VS-stage translates the guest's virtual address to a guest physical address (GPA) using the guest's page tables; the G-stage translates the GPA to a physical address using the hypervisor's Sv39x4 tables. A fault in the G-stage is a guest page fault (FD-15). GPA Guest physical address: an address a guest treats as physical, translated to a physical address by the G-stage. history length T1 to T4 use 8, 13, 32 and 119 branches of global history. IFU tb.dut.u_ifu: translation, L1I access, predecode, and delivery to the instruction buffer. instruction buffer, IBUF The queue between the IFU and decode. ITLB The instruction translation lookaside buffer: it holds recent translations from virtual to physical page numbers for fetch. A miss starts a page table walk. ITTAGE The indirect target predictor, built as TAGE is but storing targets, with its own primary and alternate (ittage_using_primary). Answers at p2. L1I tb.dut.u_l1i, 64-byte lines. Fetches from NC or IO pages are answered from memory as uncached requests (FD-18). LFSR Linear-feedback shift register: a shift register whose input is a combination of its own bits, used for a sequence of bits that looks random. Section 2 describes its use. loop predictor, LP Learns trip counts and predicts the back edge's exit. Answers at p1. misprediction A backend misprediction is a wrong-path fetch detected by the backend model, with a redirect (tb.bkend_ftq_redir_val, cause RC_MISPREDICT). A TAGE misprediction is TAGE's own direction differing from the resolved direction, whatever the final prediction was; TAGE trains and allocates on it. MSHR Miss status holding register: a register in the L1I that tracks one outstanding request to memory until it is answered. override A later prediction stage replacing an earlier one's prediction: FTB or TAGE at p2 (FD-04), SC at p3 (FD-05). It redirects the prediction request stream. p0 to p3 Prediction stages. p0: the FTQ presents a block start. p1: uBTB and loop predictor. p2: FTB, TAGE and ITTAGE. p3: SC. page fault An instruction page fault: translation of the fetch address fails, because a page table entry is invalid or does not permit execute. The fetch traps instead of delivering the instruction. page table walk Reading the page table entries for a virtual address from memory, after an ITLB miss, to find its translation. PBMT Page-based memory type (Svpbmt), a field of a leaf page table entry: normal memory, NC (non-cacheable) or IO. Code fetched from an NC or IO page is fetched uncached (FD-18). position The offset of an instruction from the start of its block, in halfwords: the instruction at the block's start is at position 0, one 6 bytes later at position 3. PPN Physical page number: a physical address without its offset within the page. predecode The IFU's step that finds the instruction boundaries and the control transfers in a block's bytes. prediction metadata Predictor state carried in the FTQ entry from prediction to update. For TAGE: the primary and alternate tables, their counters and directions, the allocation candidate, and whether the primary was the provider; returned as tage_upd_inp_u0[s].tage_pred_meta. prediction slot One branch field of an FTB entry; NUM_PRED_SLOTS (1 or 2) sets how many branches per block are predicted, slot 0 the earliest. TAGE keeps per-slot state, including use_alt_on_na. The demonstration builds a one-slot and a two-slot model (section 1). primary (TAGE) The matching tagged table with the longest history, or T0 when no tagged table matches. Table number tage_prm_comp, counter tage_prm_ctr, direction tage_prm_tkn. provider (TAGE) The table whose prediction TAGE uses: the primary, or the alternate when use_alt_on_na selects it. tage_using_primary is 1 when the primary is the provider. Which of the two provided determines how the update trains the tables. PTE Page table entry: a physical page number and permission bits, or a pointer to the next level of the table. RAS Return address stack with read and write pointers TOSR and TOSW. Each FTQ entry checkpoints them; a redirect restores the RAS from the named entry's checkpoint. redirect Sources: the BPU at p2 and p3, the IFU after predecode, and the backend on a misprediction or trap. resolution tb.bkend_ftq_rsv, one per resolved branch: FTQ index, position, direction, target, type, mispredict flag and instruction length. A conditional's target is its taken target whatever its direction. The FTQ converts resolutions into predictor updates. retire Complete an instruction in program order. In the demonstration the backend model retires an instruction when it matches the next entry of the expected execution list (section 4). SC Statistical corrector; may reverse TAGE's direction at p3. stream error A delivered instruction that does not match the expected execution list and is not explained by a misprediction. It fails the run. Sv39, Sv39x4 RISC-V page table formats. Sv39 translates 39-bit virtual addresses through three levels of tables to 4 KiB pages. Sv39x4 is the G-stage format, which translates 41-bit guest physical addresses. T0, T1 to T4 The TAGE tables: T0 the base table, T1 to T4 the tagged tables in order of increasing history length. tag, tag match A tagged table entry stores a short value formed from the branch address and the history. The entry matches a prediction request when its stored tag equals the request's. TAGE The direction predictor for conditional branches, instance tb.dut.u_bpu.u_tage. It has the base table T0 of 2-bit counters, initialized to 2'b10 (weakly taken), and four tagged tables T1 to T4, and answers at p2. tagged table A TAGE table whose entries carry a tag, so an entry answers only for the branch and history that wrote it, as far as the tag can tell them apart. TOSR, TOSW The RAS's top-of-stack read and write pointers. Each FTQ entry holds a copy of them, and a redirect restores the RAS from the copy in the entry it names. trap A transfer of control to a handler on an exception, such as a page fault or an access fault, or on an ecall. trip count The number of iterations a loop runs. uBTB Micro BTB; answers at p1. update A TAGE update arrives on tage_upd_val_u0 with tage_upd_inp_u0 and is written in the cycle trx_type is 1. Update conversion, tb.dut.u_ftq.u_upd_conv, builds each predictor's update input from a resolution and the FTQ entry's metadata. use_alt_on_na uaon, a 4-bit counter per prediction slot. When it is 8 or more and the primary is a tagged table with a weak CTR, the alternate is the provider. It is updated only when the primary and the alternate are both tagged tables. useful counter 2 bits per tagged entry, aged by period: full value in the current period, half in the next, 0 after that (ueff_p1). An entry whose aged value is 0 may be replaced by an allocation. VPN Virtual page number: a virtual address without its offset within the page. weak A CTR value of 3'b011 or 3'b100, the two values nearest the boundary between not taken and taken.

docs.title: fd01_reset_init: Reset and SRAM Initialization
docs.text:
Open waveform

Runs Surfer in the browser, with nothing to install. The signal setup takes a few seconds to apply.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
Scenario fd01_reset_init (FD01) shows the post-reset initialization of the RAMs in the TAGE, ITTAGE and SC. These branch predictor tables require an initial value before they are trained by executed branch behavior.

Initialization is done with simple FSMs that walk the table addresses writing the constants one cycle per entry. There are 2048 TAGE entries, 512 ITTAGE entries and 1024 SC entries. All tables are initialized in parallel.

Ready signals indicate to upstream logic when the predictors have completed this initialization.

This waveform shows ~2048 cycles for completion of the init process. This is followed by ~295 cycles of example requests. Lastly there are ~100 cycles before termination of the scenario.

The RAS (return address stack) initialization is also shown. The RAS init is a simple reset.

This scenario runs in the 1-prediction slot Pacino configuration. The operations are the same in either 1 or 2 prediction slots.

docs.text:
DEMO=$RVA_ROOT/examples/fe_demo

docs.title: 2. Run the scenario
docs.text:
Run simulation:

View the waveform (runs simulation first if FST is not up to date): 

make -C examples/fe_demo view S=fd01_reset_init

Console output: 

-I: fd01_reset_init : PASS : cyc = 2344

Log file output:

-I: fd01_reset_init: PASS, TAGE ready at cyc 2049, ITTAGE ready at cyc 513,
    SC ready at cyc 1025, readies seen low first 3 of 3, RAS ready at cyc 1,
    first p0 request at cyc 2049, first accepted p1 prediction at cyc 2050,
    first TAGE response at cyc 2051, first ITTAGE response at cyc 2051,
    first SC response at cyc 2052, first TAGE update at cyc 2069,
    first ITTAGE update none, first SC update at cyc 2069,
    events checked 9 of 9, cyc 2344

docs.title: 3. The program
docs.text: The program, prog_fd01, is a loop of 128 passes over 7 instructions. It only provides requests after initialization completes, and nothing in the loop depends on the initialization.

docs.title: 4. Operation
docs.text:
Signal paths are as given in section 6. Event numbers refer to section 5.

Reset is deasserted at cyc 0 (event 0). u_ftq.u_npc.w_hold is asserted because the predictors are not ready, so ftq_pred_val_p0 remains deasserted and no prediction request is issued.1

At cyc 1 (event 1) the u_sram_init FSMs of TAGE, ITTAGE and SC enter the INIT state and begin writing at address 0, with state = 2'b10. Each FSM writes one entry per cycle and all three run in parallel. u_bpu.u_ras.ras_rst_done also asserts at cyc 1, because the RAS requires only a reset.

Predictor Write enable Write cycles Entries Write data Ready asserts ITTAGE u_bpu.u_ittage.ri_wr 1 to 512 512 0 bpu_ittage_rdy, cyc 513 SC u_bpu.u_sc.tbl_ri_wr 1 to 1024 1024 0 bpu_sc_ready, cyc 1025 TAGE u_bpu.u_tage.tbl_ri_wr 1 to 2048 2048 T1-T4: 0, T0: 2'b10 bpu_tage_rdy, cyc 2049

waddr increments by one on each write and ends at the last entry of its table. In the cycle after the last write, the FSM enters the DONE state (state = 2'b11), the write enable deasserts and the predictor's ready asserts. ITTAGE and SC are ready at cyc 513 and cyc 1025 (events 2 and 3), and their ready signals remain asserted while TAGE completes.

TAGE has the largest table, so bpu_tage_rdy is the last ready to assert, at cyc 2049 (event 4). u_ftq.u_npc.w_hold deasserts in the same cycle, and the FTQ issues its first prediction request with ftq_pred_pc_p0 = 0x8000_0000. The FTQ accepts the first p1 prediction at cyc 2050 (event 5). The remaining events show the first predictor responses and the end of the run.

docs.title: 5. Events
docs.text: # cyc Event Other 0 0 reset released (tb.rstn); the FTQ withholds its p0 request (u_npc.w_hold) full init walk 1 1 the three table walks start at address 0; the RAS reset is done (ras_rst_done) each u_sram_init in INIT, waddr 0 2 513 ITTAGE ready (bpu_ittage_rdy) 512 entries 3 1025 SC ready (bpu_sc_ready) 1024 entries 4 2049 TAGE ready (bpu_tage_rdy), the last of the three; the FTQ makes its first p0 request in the same cycle 2048 entries 5 2050 first p1 prediction the FTQ accepts (w_ok_pred_p1) 6 2051 first TAGE and ITTAGE responses at p2 7 2052 first SC response at p3 8 2344 the run ends (tb.cyc_run): the last instruction retires a 100 cycle drain follows, to 2444

docs.title: fd02_steady: Steady-State Prediction and Fetch
docs.text:
Open waveform

Runs Surfer in the browser, with nothing to install. The signal setup takes a few seconds to apply.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
fd02_steady (FD-2) runs 2 KB of straight-line code. There are no branches, so every uBTB lookup will miss. Consequently the p1 prediction address returned is the fall-through address, the lookup PC + 32 bytes returned in p1 on bpu_pred_pft_p1.

In this scenario the FTQ allocates one entry per cycle. The front end reaches steady state at cyc 20, when decode begins delivering eight instructions per cycle.

The simulation executes 513 instructions, 512 addi and the halt jal. Once these instructions have retired the front end fetches for 100 more cycles, and the simulation finishes.

docs.text:

docs.title: 2. Run the scenario
docs.text:
Run simulation: 

make -C examples/fe_demo fd02_steady

View the waveform (runs simulation first if FST is not up to date): 

make -C examples/fe_demo view S=fd02_steady

Console output: 

-I: fd02_steady : PASS : cyc = 84

Log file output: 

-I: fd02_steady: PASS, allocations 83, longest allocation run 83,
    full decode bundles 64, longest bundle run 63, events checked 6 of 6, cyc 84

docs.title: 3. The program
docs.text:
Source: programs/fd02_steady.svh, task prog_fd02.

The RESET_VECTOR parameter is 0x8000_0000.

0x8000_0000   addi t0 x 512      32-bit instruction
...           (addi)             2048 bytes in 32B prediction blocks
0x8000_0800   jal x0,0           halt, loop to self

docs.title: 4. Operation
docs.text: Signal paths are as given in section 6. Event numbers refer to section 5.

docs.title: 4.1 Prediction and FTQ allocation
docs.text:
Reset is deasserted at cyc 0 (event 0). No hold condition is active, so ftq_pred_val_p0 is asserted and the FTQ issues its first prediction request, with ftq_pred_pc_p0 = 0x8000_0000 and ftq_pred_idx_p0 = 0.1

The BPU returns the p1 prediction at cyc 1 (event 1), with bpu_pred_val_p1 asserted. The uBTB lookup misses: u_bpu.r_ubtb_blk_p1.hit and bpu_pred_slot_p1.[0].slot_valid are deasserted, and bpu_pred_pft_p1 is the lookup PC + 0x20. u_ftq.w_ok_pred_p1 asserts when bpu_pred_idx_p1 matches the outstanding request, and this writes the prediction into the FTQ entry.2

In the same cycle, bpu_pred_pft_p1 drives ftq_pred_pc_p0 combinationally. This is the zero-bubble path: the next request is presented in the cycle in which the current prediction is formed, so no idle cycle separates consecutive prediction blocks.3 As a result, ftq_pred_pc_p0 increments by 0x20 per cycle and u_ftq.w_ok_pred_p1 remains asserted from cyc 1. u_ftq.u_npc.w_hold, ftq_full, u_ftq.w_ok_slot_p2 and u_ftq.w_ok_slot_p3 remain deasserted throughout.

docs.title: 4.2 Instruction fetch
docs.text:
The FTQ presents entries to the IFU from cyc 3. ftq_ifu_req_val and ftq_ifu_req_rdy are asserted, so one block transfers per cycle, with ftq_ifu_next_pc equal to ftq_ifu_start_pc + 0x20.

Each block fetch covers 34 bytes: the 32-byte block plus one halfword, for a 32-bit instruction that crosses the block end. A block that starts in the upper half of a 64-byte L1I line therefore requires two lines, and it reuses the first if the previous block requested it. Block 0x8000_0000 requests line 0x8000_0000 at cyc 4 and block 0x8000_0020 requests line 0x8000_0040 at cyc 5. Thereafter, only the upper-half blocks issue requests, so ifu_l1i_req_val asserts on odd cycles from cyc 7. l1i_ifu_rsp_val first asserts at cyc 16 and then asserts every second cycle.5

docs.title: 4.3 Delivery to decode
docs.text:
The block at 0x8000_0000 reaches the IBUF at cyc 18 (event 2). ifu_ibuf_val is asserted and u_ibuf.w_n_pres is 8, so all eight tb.pd_out.[i].valid lanes are asserted. tb.dec_ibuf_rdy is asserted, so u_ibuf.w_n_pop is also 8. Each block passes through the IBUF without accumulating, and u_ibuf.r_count remains 0.

No block is delivered at cyc 19, because block 0x8000_0020 also requires line 0x8000_0040, which is returned at cyc 18 and is readable from cyc 19. From cyc 20 (event 3) through cyc 82, one full bundle is delivered every cycle, with tb.pd_out.[0].start_pc incrementing by 0x20. This is the steady state: one line every two cycles, at two blocks per line and eight instructions per block, delivers eight instructions per cycle.

Predecode writes back to the FTQ one cycle after each bundle, with ifu_ftq_pdwb_val asserted and ifu_ftq_cfi_val deasserted until the halt. u_ftq.w_commit_ptr advances one entry per cycle from cyc 23.

docs.title: 4.4 Halt
docs.text:
Prediction continues past the halt JAL, which has not been trained into the BPU. ftq_pred_pc_p0 reaches 0x8000_0800 at cyc 64 and continues along the fall-through path to 0x8000_0a60.

The halt block reaches decode at cyc 83 (event 4). u_ibuf.w_n_pres is 1, so only lane 0 is valid. At cyc 84 the predecode writeback identifies the JAL: ifu_ftq_cfi_val and ifu_ftq_mis_val are asserted, ifu_ftq_mis_pos is 0 and ifu_ftq_target is 0x8000_0800. This asserts u_ftq.w_pd_redir_val, u_ftq.w_redir_val and ftq_ifu_flush_val, and redirects ftq_pred_pc_p0 to 0x8000_0800.

The last instruction has retired by cyc 84 (event 5), so tb.dec_ibuf_rdy deasserts.4

docs.title: 5. Events
docs.text: # cyc Event Other 0 0 reset released (tb.rstn); the FTQ requests 0x8000_0000 the same cycle fast init 1 1 first p1 prediction the FTQ accepts; one in every cycle from here to the end of the simulation uBTB miss, the next 32-byte block 2 18 first full decode bundle, the block at 0x8000_0000: all eight lanes of pd_out valid 3 20 second full bundle, the block at 0x8000_0020; one full bundle in every cycle from here to cyc 82 4 83 the halt block reaches decode, one instruction in lane 0 0x8000_0800 5 84 the last instruction retires

docs.title: FD-3 Two Branches in One Block
fd03_two_branch: Two Branches in One Block
docs.text:
Open waveform

Runs Surfer in the browser, with nothing to install. The signal setup takes a few seconds to apply.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
fd03_two_branch (FD-3) runs a loop through two regions of code, X and Y. Each region has two conditional branches, at offsets +2 and +8 from the first instruction of the region, which places both branches within one 32-byte prediction block.

After the first pass (event 5), an FTQ prediction request at X or at Y (ftq_pred_pc_p0) hits an entry holding both branches in the uBTB and in the FTB, so the p1 prediction (uBTB) and the p2 slot group (FTB) for that prediction block have both prediction slots valid.

The FTQ accepts 78 p1 predictions and 74 p2 slot groups with both slots valid. The result line in the log file reports both counts.

This scenario runs in the 2-prediction slot Pacino configuration, NUM_PRED_SLOTS=2, and both prediction slots are used.
